summary: Defines a MIB module for managing Frame Relay service level definitions, so network operators can describe and monitor the service levels of Frame Relay connections through SNMP. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: When you buy internet service, the company promises how fast and reliable it will be. This gives network tools a standard way to write down and check those promises.

questions: how to measure frame relay delay
what is a reference point in frame relay
subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for measuring Frame Relay delay, delivery ratios and availability, as defined by the Frame Relay Forum's FRF.13.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay customers and providers need to evaluate services, measure quality and enforce service level agreements, and FRF.13 defines the measurements for this but gives no standard SNMP objects for them.
tldr.mechanism: The FRSLD-MIB provides control tables that choose which reference points in the network to measure, a data table of free-running counters, and an optional sample table of historical buckets. A manager combines these counters using formulas given in the RFC to get delay, delivery ratios and availability.
tldr.outcome: Operators get one standard way to collect FRF.13 statistics for a permanent virtual connection (PVC). The unit metadata says this RFC is updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3202 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists it as updated by RFC 9141. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the MIB Module Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3202 defines the FRSLD-MIB, a MIB module for managing the Frame Relay Forum's Implementation Agreement for Service Level Definitions, known as FRF.13. It applies to interfaces of ifType frameRelay(32) and frameRelayService(44).

Service level definitions describe characteristics of a Frame Relay service that help with four tasks: evaluating providers, offerings or products; measuring quality of service; enforcing service level agreements; and planning or describing a network. The RFC does not recommend any implementation method. That is left to the device manufacturer.

The text assumes the SNMP management framework and a handful of terms: the CIR (committed information rate, the rate the network commits to deliver under normal conditions), the DLCI (data link connection identifier), the PVC (permanent virtual connection, with endpoints defined at subscription time), and UNI and NNI (user and network-to-network interfaces).
sections.plainLanguage: A company that sells you a connection makes promises about it. This document gives network tools a shared way to check those promises.

sections.title: The Four Measurements
sections.content:
FRF.13 defines four parameters, and this module supplies the objects to compute them.

  • Delay: the time from when a frame exits the source to when it reaches the destination. This MIB reports it in microseconds, although FRF.13 uses milliseconds.
  • Frame delivery ratio: frames delivered divided by frames sent, which can be split into frames within the CIR and frames in excess of the CIR.
  • Data delivery ratio: the same idea counted in octets of data rather than frames.
  • Service availability: how long the service was not available. FRF.13 defines Mean Time to Repair, Virtual Connection Availability and Mean Time Between Service Outages.

The last two availability measures need the scheduled outage time. The RFC assumes network management software keeps that, since devices often cannot track dates and moving maintenance windows, so it is not in the MIB module.
sections.plainLanguage: It keeps score on four things: how long a message takes, how many messages arrive, how much stuff arrives, and how often the line was down.

sections.title: Reference Points
sections.content:
In the RFC's network model, two Frame Relay DTE devices connect to a network cloud over UNI connections, and the cloud can contain zero or more NNI connections between networks. Calculations can be done at any reference point (RP) in this path. The RFC's figure shows source, ingress, traffic policing, egress queue input and output, and destination reference points. Proprietary reference points are also allowed anywhere not already defined.

Each PVC is watched as two one-way flows, so four reference points are needed in all. The objects frsldPvcCtrlTransmitRP and frsldPvcCtrlReceiveRP choose them. Values mix local and remote: for transmit, srcLocalRP(1) is the local source and srcRemoteRP(7) the remote source; for receive, desLocalRP(1) and desRemoteRP(7) are the destinations. A device reports only what passes its own local reference points, unless it gets remote data by some implementation-specific means. The object frsldRPCaps lists what a device can monitor.

FRF.13 names three measurement domains. In Edge-to-Edge Egress Queue, the source device uses ingTxLocalRP(2) and the destination device uses eqiRxLocalRP(4). The Edge-to-Edge Interface and End-to-End examples work similarly, ending at eqoRxLocalRP(5) and desLocalRP(1).
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine timing a package at different spots on its trip: leaving the sender, entering the post office, leaving the post office, arriving. You pick which two spots to compare.

sections.title: Setting Up and Collecting Data
sections.content:
To create rows by hand, a manager makes sure the PVC exists between the two devices, works out the reference points needed, creates rows on each device, and optionally creates sample control rows. To pick reference points, locate both devices, read frsldRPCaps on each, and find a pair that covers all the necessary points. If no pair does, the FRF.13 service level cannot be monitored. Three capability objects, frsldPvcCtrlWriteCaps, frsldSmplCtrlWriteCaps and frsldRPCaps, help with discovery. Four more (frsldMaxPvcCtrls, frsldNumPvcCtrls, frsldMaxSmplCtrls, frsldNumSmplCtrls) let a manager cap memory use.

Setting a status object to destroy(6) deletes the row, and destroying a PVC control row also destroys its sample control, sample and data rows. Rows can also be removed automatically when the DLCI they rely on disappears; the purge interval is set by frsldPvcCtrlPurge, so history can be kept briefly after removal.

There are three ways to collect data. Remote polling reads the free-running counters in the PVC data table, ideally all of one PVC's statistics in a single PDU. Sampling uses the sample tables, which hold historic buckets read with getNext or getBulk, so the manager can collect when it affects traffic least. User history from RFC 2021 is an alternative for devices that skip the sample tables.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell each device which spots to watch. Then you either ask it for the running totals now, or let it save snapshots to read later.

sections.title: Computing Delay, Ratios and Availability
sections.content:
The RFC gives the arithmetic. For delay, frsldPvcCtrlDelayType says whether the average is oneWay(1) or roundTrip(2). A round-trip average SHOULD be divided by two to get the frame transfer delay; a one-way value is used as is.

The frame delivery ratio is the frames delivered within CIR plus those in excess, divided by frames offered within CIR plus those in excess. The committed ratio divides delivered within CIR by offered within CIR, and the excess ratio does the same for the excess counts. The data delivery ratio is identical but counts octets.

For availability, mean time to repair is the unavailable time divided by the number of unavailable events, and is 0 if there were none. Virtual connection availability is the interval minus excluded time minus unavailable time, divided by the interval minus excluded time, times 100. Mean time between service outages divides that same numerator by the number of unavailable events. These formulas cover one direction of flow, and the reference points used SHOULD consistently represent data sent by one device and received by the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Divide what arrived by what was sent to see how much got through. Divide the downtime by the number of breakdowns to see how long each repair took.

sections.title: Tables in the Module
sections.content:
The module is organized as five parts. frsldPvcCtrlTable is the central control table, and a row there MUST exist before a row can exist in any other table. frsldSmplCtrlTable is an optional table that controls sampling. frsldPvcDataTable holds calculated data based on the control table. frsldPvcSampleTable holds samples of delivery and availability information plus delay calculated over the sample period. frsldCapabilities reports which read-create objects can actually be written.

The module needs ifIndex information from the IF-MIB, which is required. DLCI information can come from the Frame Relay DTE MIB or the Frame Relay Network Services MIB, but neither is required. When a control row becomes active, the DLCI can be known and active, not yet created, or just removed. In the second case the status SHOULD report notReady(3), and in the third the frsldPvcCtrlDeleteOnPurge object steers what happens.

Control table data SHOULD persist across power cycles, though a row may come back as notReady(3) if its DLCI does not. The other tables SHOULD NOT persist, since their reference timestamp would no longer be valid.
sections.plainLanguage: One table holds the settings, one holds the running scores, one holds saved snapshots, and a small one says which settings can be changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Some objects have read-write or read-create access and may be sensitive. Allowing SET operations in an unprotected environment can harm network operations. SNMPv1 alone is not secure, and even on a protected network nothing controls who may GET or SET these objects. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model, and makes it the user's responsibility to give access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can change the settings, they could mess up the network, so only the right people should be allowed.

items.title: Delay
items.text: Time from the frame leaving the source to reaching the destination, in microseconds.

items.title: Frame delivery ratio
items.text: Frames delivered divided by frames offered.

items.title: Data delivery ratio
items.text: Octets delivered divided by octets offered.

items.title: Service availability
items.text: Time the service was unavailable, via FRMTTR, FRVCA and FRMTBSO.
